decisions.title: Tenancy enforcement (non-bypassable session filter)
decisions.decision: Three cooperating layers in core/tenancy.py + core/db.py. (1) Context: a ContextVar[uuid.UUID | None] `current_tenant_id`, set exclusively by the auth dependency in core/deps.py after JWT validation and reset via token in a finally block by a pure-ASGI middleware that owns the request scope. (2) SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE filtering: a global `@event.listens_for(Session, "do_orm_execute")` hook (attached to the sync Session class — AsyncSession proxies it, so it fires for all AsyncSession.execute calls, including relationship/lazy loads). The hook adds `with_loader_criteria(TenantMixin, lambda cls: cls.tenant_id == current_tenant_id.get(), include_aliases=True, track_closure_variables=False)` to every ORM statement; with_loader_criteria also applies to ORM-enabled update()/delete(), so bulk writes are scoped too. The hook is FAIL-CLOSED: if `current_tenant_id` is unset and the statement touches any TenantMixin mapper, it raises TenancyError — unless a second ContextVar set only by the `system_context()` context manager is active. system_context() is invoked in exactly four places: the login flow (user lookup before a token exists), tenant provisioning in admin, Alembic/seed.py, and the bus when replaying system events; it is in core/tenancy.py and greppable in review. (3) Write stamping: a `before_flush` Session event stamps `obj.tenant_id = current_tenant_id.get()` on new TenantMixin objects when unset and raises TenancyError when an object's tenant_id (new or dirty) differs from the context. (4) DB backstop: every FK between tenant-scoped tables is composite `(tenant_id, <entity>_id)` referencing `UNIQUE (tenant_id, id)` on the parent, so a cross-tenant reference is impossible at the schema level on both Postgres and SQLite; declared via a `tenant_fk()` helper in core/models.py so model authors cannot get it wrong. Non-bypassability tests in tests/core/test_tenancy.py iterate `Base.registry.mappers` dynamically (new models are auto-covered): for every TenantMixin mapper, seed rows in two tenants, then assert (a) bare `session.execute(select(cls))` under tenant A returns zero tenant-B rows, (b) relationship loads never leak, (c) `update(cls)` with no WHERE only touches tenant-A rows, (d) execution with unset ContextVar raises, (e) inserting with a foreign tenant_id raises, (f) `session.get(cls, b_id)` under tenant A returns None.
decisions.rationale: do_orm_execute + with_loader_criteria is the only SQLAlchemy 2.0 mechanism that injects criteria into every ORM statement — including relationship loads and ORM bulk update/delete — without any cooperation from the query author, which is exactly the 'cannot bypass' requirement. ContextVar is async-task-safe under FastAPI's task-per-request model. Fail-closed-when-unset converts the classic 'forgot to set tenant' bug from a data leak into a hard error. Composite FKs give a database-level invariant that survives even raw SQL mistakes, and they work identically on Postgres and SQLite (D-003). Mapper-enumerating tests make the guarantee self-extending as modules are added.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS) with `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id`: rejected as the primary mechanism because the test suite and demo run on SQLite (D-003), so RLS would be unprovable in CI and would leave SQLite unprotected; noted in DECISIONS.md as a Postgres-only hardening layer post-v1. Per-query `.where(tenant_id == ...)` helpers or a custom Query base class: bypassable by any author who writes select() directly. Schema-per-tenant / database-per-tenant: contradicts the mandated row-level tenant_id design and makes cross-tenant ops (provisioning, platform analytics) and Alembic management disproportionately heavy. Mapper-level events only (before_insert/before_update) without do_orm_execute: guards writes but not reads.
decisions.risks: Raw `session.execute(text(...))` and Core-table inserts bypass the ORM hook — mitigated by a CI grep gate banning `text(` and `.insert()` outside core/, the composite-FK backstop, and code review; document the residual gap in DECISIONS.md. Objects already in the identity map are returned by session.get() without SQL — benign because the per-request session only ever contains same-tenant rows, but sessions must never be shared across requests (enforced by the request-scoped session dependency). track_closure_variables=False is required so the lambda re-reads the ContextVar per execution rather than baking in the first value seen.

decisions.title: Auth token flow (JWT access+refresh, argon2)
decisions.decision: PyJWT with HS256 and a single `ATLAS_SECRET_KEY` (env, ≥64 random bytes). Access token: 15-min TTL, claims {sub: user_id, tenant_id, sid: refresh-session id, ver: user.token_version, typ: "access", jti, iat, exp}; stateless — no DB lookup for revocation, but `ver` is compared to the user row (loaded anyway for RBAC) so 'revoke all my sessions' = increment core_users.token_version. No roles/permissions embedded in the token. Refresh token: JWT, 14-day TTL, claims {sub, tenant_id, sid, typ: "refresh", jti, exp}, delivered as an httpOnly Secure SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to path /api/v1/auth; access token returned in the JSON body and held in memory by the SPA. Server-side state: table core_refresh_sessions (id uuid = sid, tenant_id, user_id, current_jti_hash sha256 text, issued_at, last_used_at, expires_at, revoked_at nullable, ip, user_agent). Rotation with reuse detection: POST /api/v1/auth/refresh verifies signature+typ, loads the session row by sid; jti-hash match → issue new access+refresh pair and UPDATE current_jti_hash (single UPDATE ... WHERE sid=? AND current_jti_hash=? so concurrent refreshes race safely — the loser gets 0 rows and a 401); jti mismatch → token replay: set revoked_at on the whole session (family) and return 401. Logout revokes the sid row. Login (POST /api/v1/auth/login, body: tenant_slug + email + password) runs under system_context() to resolve tenant + user. Passwords: argon2-cffi PasswordHasher(type=argon2id, time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536 KiB, parallelism=4) per RFC 9106; verify/hash executed via anyio.to_thread.run_sync so the event loop never blocks; check_needs_rehash() on every successful login upgrades old hashes. FastAPI side in core/deps.py: HTTPBearer security scheme → `get_current_user` dependency decodes, validates typ/exp/ver, sets the tenancy ContextVar, returns a frozen CurrentUser dataclass (user_id, tenant_id, permissions frozenset); routers depend on it directly or via require_permission().
decisions.rationale: HS256 is sufficient and simplest for a single-service monolith — no key distribution problem exists. 15-min stateless access tokens keep the hot path DB-free for token validation while the ver claim gives an emergency global-revoke valve at zero extra query cost. Storing only the hash of the current refresh jti (not the token) means a DB leak cannot mint sessions, and single-row compare-and-swap rotation gives airtight replay detection (the OAuth 'refresh token rotation with automatic reuse detection' pattern). Cookie-held refresh + memory-held access is the standard XSS/CSRF compromise for SPAs. The argon2 parameters are the RFC 9106 recommended settings and argon2-cffi's defaults neighborhood; thread offload is mandatory because argon2id at 64 MiB takes tens of ms.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: RS256/EdDSA asymmetric keys: pays key-management cost for a consumer (the same process) that doesn't exist; revisit only if tokens are ever validated by a second service. Opaque random refresh tokens in DB: marginally simpler but the constraint specifies JWT access+refresh; JWT refresh also lets us reject garbage before any DB hit. Redis denylist for access-token revocation: adds an infrastructure dependency the stack doesn't have; 15-min exposure + ver bump is an acceptable v1 envelope. Storing refresh tokens in localStorage: XSS-exfiltratable. bcrypt: explicitly overridden by the argon2 constraint.
decisions.risks: Symmetric key compromise forges any token — mitigated by env-only storage, never logging tokens, and short access TTL. Refresh-rotation race on flaky networks (client refreshes, response lost, retries with old jti) triggers family revocation and forces re-login — accepted as fail-safe behavior; last_used_at + a 10-second grace window can be added later if it bites. SameSite=Strict assumes the SPA and API share a site; document that a split-origin deploy must move to SameSite=None + CSRF token.

decisions.title: RBAC data model + permission dependency + field masking
decisions.decision: Four tables. core_permissions (id, key text UNIQUE like 'finance.journal.post', description) — a GLOBAL, code-defined catalog: each module declares its permission keys as constants in constants.py, a registry in core/rbac.py collects them, and a startup sync (and seed.py) upserts the catalog; permissions are not tenant-editable data. core_roles (id, tenant_id, name, description, is_system bool; UNIQUE(tenant_id, name)) — tenant-scoped, with template-provided system roles seeded at tenant provisioning. core_role_permissions (role_id, permission_id, composite PK). core_user_roles (tenant_id, user_id, role_id, composite PK). Permission check: `require_permission(key: str)` factory in core/rbac.py returns an async dependency that depends on get_current_user; effective permissions are resolved once per request by one query (user_roles ⋈ role_permissions ⋈ permissions) and memoized in an in-process TTL cache (60 s) keyed (tenant_id, user_id, token_version); miss → 403 with error envelope code 'permission_denied' naming the missing key. Routers attach it per route: `@router.post("/{id}/post", dependencies=[Depends(require_permission(FIN_JOURNAL_POST))])`. The resolved frozenset also lands on CurrentUser and in a `current_permissions` ContextVar set by get_current_user. Field-level read masking (HR compensation/IDs): a reusable annotated type in core/schemas.py — `Masked(permission: str)` implemented as `Annotated[T | None, WrapSerializer(_mask_serializer), MaskedMeta(permission)]`; the wrap serializer reads the `current_permissions` ContextVar at serialization time and returns the real value only if the required key (e.g. 'hr.employee.read_compensation') is present, else None. Because it keys off a ContextVar, it works under FastAPI's response_model serialization without plumbing SerializationInfo.context. Write side: routers for masked fields require the corresponding update permission via require_permission, and the Update schema excludes masked fields into a separate endpoint/schema so a partial update can never silently null compensation.
decisions.rationale: Roles→permissions→resources 'as data' is satisfied by tenant-scoped roles and assignments, while keeping the permission catalog code-owned prevents tenants from inventing keys no code checks. One resolution query + short TTL cache makes per-route checks O(1) without embedding stale permissions in JWTs (revocation takes effect within 60 s or instantly on token_version bump). The Annotated + WrapSerializer approach is idiomatic Pydantic v2, declarative at the schema (the field itself names its guarding permission), and centralizes masking in exactly one core construct — module authors cannot re-implement it inconsistently. Masking to None (not '***') keeps response types honest for the TypeScript mirror (field: number | null).
decisions.risks: ContextVar-dependent serialization means dumping schemas outside a request (tests, background jobs) sees no permissions and masks everything — fail-closed and correct, but tests must set the ContextVar fixture explicitly. TTL cache means a permission grant/revoke can lag up to 60 s — documented; admin 'revoke now' bumps token_version which changes the cache key immediately. Masked-to-None is ambiguous with genuinely-null compensation for authorized readers — acceptable for v1; if it bites, add a sibling boolean is_masked computed in the same serializer.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Embedding permissions in the JWT: stale for 15 min after role changes and bloats the token; rejected since the user row is loaded anyway. Per-tenant permission catalog: invites orphan keys no code enforces. Casbin/oso policy engines: external DSLs fight the 'RBAC as data + service layer owns logic' rule and complicate the SQLite/Postgres story. computed_field/model_post_init masking on each HR schema: scatters security logic across modules. FastAPI response_model_exclude per-route: route-level, not principal-level, and silently drifts from schemas.

decisions.title: Audit capture (session-event diffs + middleware context)
decisions.decision: Both layers, with disjoint responsibilities. Data layer (core/audit.py): SQLAlchemy Session events. An `after_flush` listener walks session.new / session.dirty / session.deleted for auditable models (AuditMixin), computing per-column diffs from `inspect(obj).attrs[col].history` (update: {field: {old, new}} for changed columns only; insert: new values; delete: old values), skipping columns named in the model's `__audit_exclude__` tuple (password_hash always; HR compensation fields are INCLUDED but the audit viewer masks them with the same Masked machinery). Rows are buffered on session.info and written in `after_flush_postexec` via a single Core `session.execute(insert(core_audit_log), rows)` on the same connection — inside the same transaction, so audit is atomic with the change: rollback removes both, commit persists both, and no business write can commit without its audit row. Context layer: a pure-ASGI middleware creates a RequestContext (request_id uuid, ip from X-Forwarded-For with trusted-proxy handling, user_agent, method+path) into a ContextVar at request start; get_current_user later fills actor_user_id and tenant_id on the same object; the flush listener reads it (absent context ⇒ actor NULL, marked source='system' for seed/jobs). Table core_audit_log: id bigint identity PK, tenant_id nullable, actor_user_id nullable, source text ('http'|'system'), action text ('insert'|'update'|'delete'), entity_table text, entity_id text, diff JSON (JSONB on Postgres via the JSON().with_variant pattern per D-003), request_id, ip text, created_at timestamptz default now. Indexed (tenant_id, entity_table, entity_id, created_at). Append-only enforced at THREE levels: (a) no service/repository code path performs update/delete on the model and the model registers no update API; (b) DB triggers created in the Alembic migration with dialect branching — Postgres: a trigger function raising EXCEPTION on UPDATE OR DELETE; SQLite: `CREATE TRIGGER ... BEFORE UPDATE ON core_audit_log BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'audit is append-only'); END` plus the DELETE twin; (c) on Postgres deployments, REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE on the table from the app role in the same migration. core_audit_log itself is excluded from audit capture and carries TenantMixin so the admin audit viewer is tenant-filtered for free.
decisions.rationale: Session events are the only layer that sees true before/after column values (HTTP middleware sees payloads, not prior DB state, and misses service-internal writes like event-handler postings). Middleware is the only layer that knows transport facts. Splitting exactly along that line satisfies 'written by middleware, not per-endpoint code' in spirit — zero per-endpoint code — while making the diff source authoritative. Same-transaction writes make the audit trail exactly as trustworthy as the ledger itself. Trigger-based append-only works identically under the SQLite test run, so the guarantee is provable in CI (a test attempts UPDATE/DELETE and asserts the raise).
decisions.alternatives_rejected: HTTP-middleware-only auditing (capture request/response bodies): cannot produce before/after diffs, misses event-bus side effects, and bloats storage with payloads. Postgres-only audit triggers capturing OLD/NEW row JSON: invisible to SQLite CI and duplicates logic per table. before_flush capture: history is reliable there too, but generated PKs for new objects aren't assigned yet — after_flush sees final PKs. Outbox/async audit writer: breaks atomicity between change and audit record.
decisions.risks: after_flush_postexec inserts must use Core insert (ORM adds there would dirty the unit of work) — enforced by a comment-anchored test that audits rows during a multi-flush transaction. Bulk ORM update()/delete() statements bypass flush events and thus audit — v1 policy: services must mutate via loaded objects for auditable entities; a do_orm_execute assertion raises if a bulk write targets an AuditMixin mapper, turning silent gaps into errors. Diff JSON of large text columns can bloat the table — cap per-field diff size with truncation marker.

decisions.title: Domain-event bus (sync, in-transaction dispatch)
decisions.decision: core/events.py defines: DomainEvent base (Pydantic v2 model, frozen) with ClassVar `key` ('sales.order.shipped'), plus tenant_id and occurred_at fields; an EventBus Protocol with `publish(session, event)` and a `@subscribe(key)` decorator; and the v1 implementation InProcessEventBus. Semantics — collect-then-dispatch, inside the same DB transaction: services call `bus.publish(session, event)`, which appends to a FIFO buffer in session.info['pending_events'] (no immediate dispatch, so a service's own invariants are settled first). The request unit-of-work (the session dependency in core/deps.py that wraps the service call) drains the buffer after the service returns and before commit: pop events FIFO, for each event run its handlers synchronously in deterministic order (handler registration order = the fixed module import order in main.py's app factory, mirroring the build order: finance, inventory, procurement, sales, ...), passing (event, session) so handlers write into the SAME transaction; handlers may publish further events, which append to the same queue (breadth-first), with a hard depth counter (max 50 dispatches per transaction) raising EventCycleError. Then one commit. Handler failure semantics: any handler exception propagates, the whole transaction rolls back, the API returns the error envelope — deliberately NO isolation: if SalesOrderShipped's COGS posting fails, the goods issue must not commit, because financial consistency (universal-journal atomicity) outranks availability. Modules register handlers only in their handlers.py via @subscribe, importing event classes from the publishing module's events.py (the one permitted cross-module import besides queries.py). Swappability: business code only ever touches `bus.publish` and @subscribe with JSON-serializable Pydantic events; the migration path to Kafka/Redis is a TransactionalOutboxBus implementing the same Protocol that writes core_event_outbox rows (event key + payload JSON) in the same transaction and lets a relay process ship them — zero changes in modules.
decisions.rationale: Dispatch-in-transaction is the only semantics that upholds rule 8.1/8.7 of CLAUDE.md: cross-module financial effects (goods issue → COGS journal) must be all-or-nothing with their trigger, and an in-process sync bus sharing the session gives exactly-once, atomic causality with no outbox/relay machinery in v1. Buffering until the service returns (rather than dispatching mid-service) means handlers observe a consistent aggregate state and the publisher's own validation completes first. Deterministic ordering makes test output and ledger line order reproducible. Pydantic-serializable events plus a Protocol interface is precisely the seam Kafka needs later.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: After-commit dispatch: decouples failures, but a crashed handler then leaves shipped stock with no COGS posting and no automatic remediation — unacceptable for financial invariants without an outbox+retry system, which is post-v1 scope. Immediate (publish-time) dispatch: handlers would interleave with the publisher's half-finished writes. Per-handler error isolation (catch, log, continue): converts consistency bugs into silent data divergence. Celery/background tasks for handlers: loses the transaction entirely and adds infrastructure the stack forbids.
decisions.risks: Long synchronous chains extend request latency and transaction hold time (lock duration on the numbering row, SQLite write lock) — mitigated by the depth cap, by keeping handlers thin (post + publish, no I/O beyond the session), and by a per-dispatch debug log of the chain. A handler needing data from a module it precedes in the dependency order must use that module's queries.py, never the session against foreign models — enforced by import-linting in CI. Non-transactional side effects (email) must NOT ride this bus; the seam for them is a later after-commit hook, recorded now in DECISIONS.md so nobody bolts SMTP into a handler.

decisions.title: Document flow schema (registry + link table)
decisions.decision: Two core tables plus a mixin, in core/docflow.py + core/models.py. core_documents — the registry: id uuid PK, tenant_id, doc_type text (namespaced constant like 'sales.order', 'inv.goods_receipt', 'fin.journal_entry' — declared in each module's constants.py and collected in a core registry like permissions), doc_no text (from the numbering service), status text, created_at; UNIQUE(tenant_id, doc_type, doc_no); UNIQUE(tenant_id, id) to serve composite tenant FKs. Every business document table (sls_orders, fin_journal_entries, …) carries document_id uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE referencing core_documents — a real FK, applied via a DocumentMixin; the row is created by `docflow.register(session, doc_type, doc_no)` inside the service that creates the document. core_doc_links — the edges: predecessor_id and successor_id both FK → core_documents.id, link_type text ('fulfills', 'invoices', 'reverses', 'posts'), quantity Numeric nullable and amount/currency_code nullable for partial-fulfillment quantities, created_at; PK(predecessor_id, successor_id, link_type); CHECK(predecessor_id != successor_id); tenant_id with the composite-FK pattern. Links are written by the service creating the successor (e.g. delivery creation links order→delivery) — usually inside event handlers or the same service call. Traversal: `docflow.get_chain(session, document_id)` runs ONE recursive CTE per direction (`WITH RECURSIVE` — supported by both Postgres and SQLite ≥3.8.3, expressed with SQLAlchemy's select().cte(recursive=True)): ancestors walk predecessor edges, descendants walk successor edges, each carrying a depth column capped at 20 and a visited-path string for cycle safety; result is merged into a {nodes: [{id, doc_type, doc_no, status}], edges: [{from, to, link_type, quantity}]} payload that GET /api/v1/core/documents/{id}/flow returns verbatim for the DocFlowViewer component. Display metadata beyond the registry columns (e.g. amounts) is resolved by a per-doc_type summary callback each module registers, called only for the nodes in the chain.
decisions.rationale: A registry table turns the polymorphic (doc_type, doc_id) problem into ordinary FK integrity: link rows can never dangle, UNIQUE(tenant_id, doc_type, doc_no) gives the numbering invariant a home, and chain traversal is a single self-join CTE over one narrow table regardless of how many document types exist — the UI requirement ('render the full chain for any document') becomes one generic endpoint. Business FKs (delivery.order_id) still exist for domain logic; doc flow is an additive uniform graph, exactly the ACDOCA-era document-relationship-browser shape the parity doc commits to.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Bare polymorphic pairs (doc_type, doc_id) in the link table without a registry: no FK enforcement on either end, every traversal needs a per-type join fan-out, and tenant scoping must be re-verified per edge. Per-table FK links only (order_id on delivery, etc.): chain traversal would require N module-aware queries in core, violating the core-imports-nothing-from-modules rule. Single-table inheritance for all documents: forces every document's columns into one table or heavy joined inheritance — far too invasive. Materialized closure table for traversal speed: premature; chains are short (<10 nodes) and the CTE is cheap.
decisions.risks: Dual-write discipline (business row + registry row + link rows in one transaction) could be forgotten by a module author — mitigated by DocumentMixin making document_id NOT NULL (the insert fails without registration) and a shared test helper asserting chain integrity for each module's happy path. The registry's status column can drift from the business table's status — rule: modules update it through docflow.set_status() in the same transaction; a reconciliation assertion runs in tests. SQLite recursive-CTE performance is fine at demo scale; the depth-20 cap bounds pathological graphs.

decisions.title: Idempotency keys (storage, scoping, replay)
decisions.decision: Table core_idempotency_keys: tenant_id, key text (client-supplied `Idempotency-Key` header, max 200 chars), endpoint text (METHOD + route template, e.g. 'POST /api/v1/finance/journal-entries'), request_hash text (sha256 of the canonical JSON body), status text ('in_progress'|'completed'), response_status int nullable, response_body JSON nullable, created_at, completed_at nullable; PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, endpoint, key). Scope is tenant+endpoint+key: the same key value on two different endpoints is two reservations, preventing accidental cross-endpoint collisions from client-side key reuse. Flow, implemented as a single dependency `idempotency_guard(required=True)` in core/deps.py applied to flagged routes: (1) reservation transaction — INSERT the (tenant, endpoint, key, request_hash, 'in_progress') row and COMMIT immediately in its own short transaction so concurrent duplicates collide on the PK on both Postgres and SQLite (SQLite's single-writer lock serializes them anyway); on conflict, read the existing row: status='in_progress' and age < 5 min → 409 code 'idempotency_in_progress' (client retries later); 'in_progress' and stale (>5 min, a crashed attempt) → take over by compare-and-swap on created_at; 'completed' with matching request_hash → REPLAY: return the stored response_status + response_body verbatim with header `Idempotency-Replayed: true`, executing no business logic; 'completed' with different request_hash → 422 code 'idempotency_key_reuse'. (2) Business transaction — the endpoint runs normally; in the same transaction as the business commit, the dependency's epilogue UPDATEs the row to completed with the serialized success response (2xx only; on business failure/rollback the row is deleted in a cleanup transaction so the client may retry with the same key). Required (400 'idempotency_key_required' if the header is missing) on every endpoint that creates a financial or stock document, per CLAUDE.md: journal-entry post, AP/AR invoice create, payment create/run, goods receipt, goods issue, stock transfer, count posting, delivery create/post, customer invoice create, production order confirm/finish, RMA credit note — concretely any router that calls numbering for a posting doc_type declares `dependencies=[Depends(idempotency_guard())]`. Optional (honored if sent) on master-data creates. Rows expire after 24 h; purge runs in the seed/maintenance command and lazily on collision with an expired row.
decisions.rationale: PK-arbitrated reservation-then-execute is the only pattern that is race-proof on both engines without advisory locks (Postgres unique index arbitrates; SQLite's writer lock serializes). Committing 'completed' atomically with the business transaction guarantees the cardinal invariant: a replayable success response exists if and only if the document exists. Hash comparison distinguishes safe retries from client bugs. Scoping by endpoint keeps semantics obvious and makes the same UUID-per-form-submission strategy safe in the frontend.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Single-transaction approach (reserve and execute in one txn): two concurrent duplicates would both proceed and one would fail only at commit with a confusing PK error, and on Postgres the second request blocks on the row lock for the full duration of the first's business work. Redis-based keys: forbidden infrastructure. Deriving idempotency from natural keys (e.g. external doc number): not generalizable and pushes the problem into every service. Global key scope (tenant+key only): one client key-generation bug across two endpoints would replay the wrong response.
decisions.risks: Stored response replay returns stale representations if the document changed after creation — accepted and standard (Stripe semantics); the response contains the id, clients re-fetch for current state. Takeover of stale 'in_progress' rows could double-execute if the original worker is alive-but-slow past 5 min — mitigated because the original's completed-UPDATE uses WHERE status='in_progress' AND request matches and its business commit will fail the CAS, rolling it back; the window is documented. Response bodies in JSON columns bloat the table — 24 h expiry plus purge bounds it.

decisions.title: API envelope (cursor pagination + error shape)
decisions.decision: Both shapes live in core/schemas.py. List envelope: `{"items": [...], "next_cursor": str|null, "limit": int}` — no total counts (counting defeats keyset pagination; a separate aggregate endpoint serves dashboards). Mechanics: keyset (seek) pagination, never OFFSET. Every list query orders by a whitelisted sort column plus `id` as mandatory unique tiebreaker, e.g. ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC; the page query fetches limit+1 rows (default 50, max 200 via `?limit=`); if limit+1 arrived, next_cursor is emitted from the last returned row. Cursor encoding: base64url(JSON) of {"v": 1, "k": [<last sort value, ISO-serialized>, <last id>], "s": "created_at:desc", "q": sha256-prefix-of-normalized-filters} — the cursor is OPAQUE to clients but self-describing to the server; on receipt the server validates v, validates that s and q match the request's current sort/filters (mismatch → 400 code 'cursor_invalid' instead of silently weird pages), and applies the seek predicate `(sort_col, id) < (:k0, :k1)` — written as the expanded boolean form `sort_col < :k0 OR (sort_col = :k0 AND id < :k1)` because SQLite does not support row-value comparison with mixed directions and this form is portable and index-friendly on both engines. One generic helper `paginate(session, stmt, sort, cursor, limit)` in core/schemas.py/db.py implements all of it; module routers never hand-roll pagination. Error envelope (every non-2xx, no exceptions): `{"error": {"code": str, "message": str, "details": list|null, "request_id": str}}`. `code` is machine-readable and dot-namespaced for domain rules ('finance.period_closed', 'finance.journal_unbalanced', 'idempotency_key_reuse') and generic for transport ('validation_error', 'not_found', 'permission_denied', 'unauthorized', 'conflict', 'internal_error'). core/exceptions.py defines the AtlasError hierarchy (NotFoundError→404, PermissionDeniedError→403, ConflictError→409, DomainRuleError(code, message)→422, TenancyError→403) and registers FastAPI exception handlers for AtlasError, RequestValidationError (mapped to code 'validation_error' with details=[{field, message, type}] flattened from Pydantic's errors()), and a catch-all 500 handler that logs with request_id and returns a body-free 'internal_error' message. request_id comes from the audit middleware's RequestContext and is also echoed as an X-Request-Id response header on every response.
decisions.rationale: Keyset pagination is O(page) regardless of depth, stable under concurrent inserts (no row skipping/duplication, the ERP norm for ledgers), and works identically on both engines with the expanded predicate. Encoding sort+filter fingerprints into the cursor catches the classic client bug of changing filters mid-pagination. A single error shape with machine codes lets the frontend apiClient.ts implement one error path and lets tests assert on codes rather than messages; request_id ties any user-reported error to the audit/log trail.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: OFFSET/LIMIT pagination: degrades linearly and produces phantom/duplicate rows under concurrent posting — unacceptable for journal browsing. Signed/HMAC cursors: integrity isn't a security boundary here (the seek values are data the client already saw) and validation-by-fingerprint already rejects malformed use; HMAC adds key management for no threat. RFC 7807 problem+json: fine standard, but the prescribed single envelope is simpler and the constraint says 'consistent error envelope', not problem details; we keep the door open by never colliding field names. Total-count in every list response: forces a COUNT(*) per page over million-row journals.
decisions.risks: Keyset cannot jump to arbitrary page N — accepted; the UI uses infinite scroll/next-page semantics per the design system's DataGrid. Sorting by mutable columns (e.g. status) can re-show a row that moved — documented; default sorts use immutable created_at/doc_no. The expanded seek predicate needs a composite index per supported sort column — the whitelist per endpoint is small and indexes are declared alongside it.

decisions.title: Per-tenant document numbering (gapless counter rows)
decisions.decision: Gapless-by-construction for ALL document types, via counter rows updated inside the same transaction that creates the document. Table core_number_sequences: tenant_id, doc_type text, year int (fiscal/calendar year for resetting types, 0 for non-resetting), prefix text, pattern text (Python format string, default '{prefix}-{year}-{seq:05d}'), next_no int NOT NULL default 1, padding int default 5; PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, doc_type, year). core/numbering.py exposes one async function `next_document_number(session, doc_type, year=None) -> str`: (1) ensure the row exists with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, doc_type, year) DO NOTHING (supported by both Postgres and SQLite ≥3.24); (2) claim the number with a single atomic `UPDATE core_number_sequences SET next_no = next_no + 1 WHERE tenant_id=:t AND doc_type=:d AND year=:y RETURNING next_no - 1, prefix, pattern, padding` (RETURNING is supported on Postgres and SQLite ≥3.35, which the Python 3.12 baseline ships; a tested fallback path does SELECT-then-UPDATE, safe under SQLite because its database-level write lock serializes writers anyway); (3) format via the pattern → 'INV-2026-00042'. Locking semantics: on Postgres the UPDATE takes a row lock on the (tenant, doc_type, year) counter row, serializing concurrent claimants for milliseconds; because the claim happens in the SAME transaction as the document insert, a rollback rolls the counter back too — no gaps, ever, without any reconciliation machinery. On SQLite the single-writer lock provides the same serialization trivially. The numbering call is made by the document-creating service immediately before docflow.register(), and UNIQUE(tenant_id, doc_type, doc_no) on core_documents is the DB backstop that any bug surfaces as a constraint violation, not a silent duplicate. Sequence configuration (prefix, pattern, padding, yearly reset on/off) is tenant-editable data surfaced in the admin module (PLAN Phase 14) and seeded by industry templates; doc_type keys reuse the docflow registry constants. Year rollover needs no job: the first posting of the new year inserts the new counter row on demand.
decisions.rationale: Claiming inside the committing transaction makes gaplessness a free consequence of ACID instead of a feature: the counter increment and the document are atomic, so there is no 'burned number' state to reconcile. One mechanism for all document types (instead of gapless-for-invoices, gappy-for-POs) is simpler to implement, test, and explain, and audit-friendliness/legal expectations (invoice and journal numbering) are satisfied automatically. The hot-row UPDATE pattern is the textbook portable approach — it needs no Postgres sequences (which are non-transactional and gap-prone) and no SQLite-specific code beyond the RETURNING capability check.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: PostgreSQL SEQUENCE / SERIAL: non-transactional (gaps on rollback by design), not per-tenant without dynamic sequence creation, and nonexistent on SQLite — fails three requirements at once. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE then UPDATE: works on Postgres but FOR UPDATE is a no-op syntax error risk on SQLite; the bare atomic UPDATE achieves the same lock with one statement. UUID/ULID document identifiers as the business number: humans, auditors and printed documents need short sortable numbers; UUIDs remain the internal PKs. Allocating numbers from a cached block per process: gap-prone on restart and pointless at v1 concurrency.
decisions.risks: The counter row is a serialization point: heavy concurrent posting of one doc_type in one tenant queues on the row lock — acceptable at v1 scale (milliseconds per claim) and the documented later path is switching specific non-legal doc_types to cached ranges, which only changes numbering.py. Long-running transactions that claim a number early then do slow work hold the lock — convention: claim the number as late as possible in the service, enforced in review. Pattern strings are tenant data fed to str.format — restricted by validating patterns against a whitelist of fields ({prefix},{year},{seq}) at write time to prevent format-string injection.

decisions.title: Universal journal schema (entry + line tables, dimensions, currencies, DDL invariants, reversal)
decisions.decision: Two tables in modules/finance/models.py. Header `fin_journal_entries`: `id` (sa.Uuid, app-generated UUID, portable PG-native/SQLite-CHAR), `tenant_id` (TenantMixin, indexed), `entry_number` (from core/numbering.py; UNIQUE (tenant_id, entry_number)), `document_type` (string enum: MANUAL, AP_INVOICE, AR_INVOICE, PAYMENT, COGS, FX_REVAL, DEPRECIATION, REVERSAL...), `status` (DRAFT|POSTED|REVERSED), `posting_date` (Date), `fiscal_period_id` FK→fin_fiscal_periods, `currency_code` (one transaction currency per entry — cross-currency business events become multiple entries), `functional_currency_code`, `exchange_rate` NUMERIC(20,10), `description`, `idempotency_key` (UNIQUE (tenant_id, idempotency_key) partial WHERE NOT NULL), `posted_at`, `posted_by_user_id`, `reversal_of_entry_id` self-FK (UNIQUE — an entry is reversed at most once), `reversed_by_entry_id` self-FK. Lines `fin_journal_lines`: `id` Uuid, `tenant_id`, `entry_id` FK, `line_number` (UNIQUE (entry_id, line_number)), `account_id` FK NOT NULL, and nullable dimension FKs on EVERY line (ACDOCA-style): `cost_center_id`, `profit_center_id`, `wbs_element_id` (projects), `item_id`, `vendor_id`, `customer_id` (two typed FKs, not polymorphic — masters are separate per parity doc), `warehouse_id`, `tax_code_id`, plus `quantity` + `uom_code` for material lines. Currency columns per line: `debit_amount`, `credit_amount` (transaction currency) and `functional_debit_amount`, `functional_credit_amount` (functional currency), all NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 using the MoneyType from the money decision. Denormalized onto lines for projection speed: `posting_date`, `fiscal_period_id`, `is_posted` boolean (flipped inside the posting transaction, before the header status flip). DDL constraints: (1) named CHECK `ck_fin_journal_lines_one_side`: `(debit_amount > 0 AND credit_amount = 0) OR (credit_amount > 0 AND debit_amount = 0)`; companion CHECK that functional amounts are non-negative, not both positive, and on the same side as the transaction side (functional zero allowed for sub-minor-unit rounding). (2) Balance debits==credits per entry per currency: service validates sum(debit)==sum(credit) in BOTH transaction and functional amounts before posting (a residual functional rounding cent is posted to a configured rounding-difference account so functional sums balance exactly); at DB level a row-spanning CHECK is impossible, so a per-dialect trigger on `fin_journal_entries` BEFORE UPDATE WHEN OLD.status<>'POSTED' AND NEW.status='POSTED' computes SELECT SUM over the entry's lines for both currency pairs and raises (`RAISE EXCEPTION 'ATLAS_UNBALANCED_ENTRY'` in plpgsql; `SELECT RAISE(ABORT,'ATLAS_UNBALANCED_ENTRY')` in SQLite) on mismatch — exact because both backends store exact types per the money decision. (3) Immutability of posted entries: per-dialect triggers — BEFORE UPDATE and BEFORE DELETE on `fin_journal_lines` raise 'ATLAS_POSTED_IMMUTABLE' when the parent entry status='POSTED'; BEFORE INSERT on lines raises when parent already POSTED; BEFORE DELETE on `fin_journal_entries` raises when status='POSTED'; BEFORE UPDATE on posted headers raises UNLESS the only change is `reversed_by_entry_id` NULL→value and `status` POSTED→REVERSED (the single sanctioned mutation). Posting order inside one transaction: service validation → UPDATE lines (set is_posted, posting_date, fiscal_period_id — parent still DRAFT so immutability triggers pass) → UPDATE header to POSTED (fires balance + period triggers) → audit row → domain event `finance.journal.posted`. (4) Reversal mechanics: `post_reversal(entry_id, reversal_date, reason)` in finance/service/journal.py creates a NEW entry (document_type=REVERSAL, fresh entry_number, reversal_of_entry_id set) with every line copied dimension-identical and debit/credit swapped in both currencies (original functional amounts, NOT re-translated), posted into an open period at reversal_date; then sets original.reversed_by_entry_id + status=REVERSED; both linked in core docflow. No deletes, no in-place edits, ever.
decisions.rationale: This is the ACDOCA pattern the parity doc declares load-bearing: one append-only line table carrying all FI and CO dimensions so every report is a projection. Dimensions as nullable FK columns (not EAV) keep them indexable and join-free for the margin/cost-center projections. Two amount-pair columns (transaction + functional) match the parity scope ('transaction + functional currency only' in v1) and leave room to add group-currency columns later exactly as the parity doc's 'later path' prescribes. The status-transition trigger is the only portable way to get a row-spanning balance guarantee into the DB on both backends, and it fires exactly once at the moment the invariant must hold. Denormalized posting_date/is_posted on lines makes statements single-table index scans.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Signed single `amount` column with a side enum — rejected because the prompt and CLAUDE.md hardcode the exactly-one-of-debit/credit CHECK, and signed amounts complicate trial-balance semantics. Polymorphic partner (partner_type + partner_id) — rejected: not FK-enforceable, and the parity doc deliberately keeps separate vendor/customer masters in v1. Postgres DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED constraint triggers for balance — rejected as the primary mechanism because SQLite has no deferred constraint triggers; the status-transition trigger gives identical semantics on both. Editable-until-printed entries (Odoo style) — rejected; CLAUDE.md rule 8 mandates immutable posted entries with reversal-only correction.
decisions.risks: Trigger logic duplicated per dialect can drift — mitigated by keeping both DDL strings side by side in one Alembic revision and a shared test module (tests/modules/finance/test_journal_db_guards.py) that attempts raw-SQL UPDATE/DELETE/unbalanced-post against both backends in CI. The single-allowed-header-mutation trigger (reversed_by) is the subtlest piece; it gets explicit column-by-column OLD/NEW comparison in the trigger WHEN clause and dedicated tests. Line-count blowup from denormalized columns is accepted — it is the S/4HANA trade.

decisions.title: Period-close enforcement at DB level on both dialects
decisions.decision: Table `fin_fiscal_periods`: `id`, `tenant_id`, `fiscal_year` int, `period_no` int (1–12, 13 reserved for year-end adjustments later), `start_date`, `end_date`, `status` string enum OPEN|CLOSED, UNIQUE (tenant_id, fiscal_year, period_no), CHECK start_date <= end_date. Since CHECK constraints cannot reference other tables, the portable mechanism is hand-written per-dialect triggers shipped in an Alembic migration via `op.execute()` branched on `op.get_bind().dialect.name`. Exact behavior: trigger `trg_fin_entries_period_open` BEFORE UPDATE ON fin_journal_entries, firing only on the DRAFT→POSTED transition (WHEN NEW.status='POSTED' AND OLD.status<>'POSTED'), plus a twin BEFORE INSERT trigger guarding direct inserts WHERE status='POSTED' (defense in depth — the service never inserts posted). Body: look up the period row `WHERE tenant_id = NEW.tenant_id AND NEW.posting_date BETWEEN start_date AND end_date`; if no row exists OR status<>'OPEN', abort with message 'ATLAS_PERIOD_CLOSED'. Postgres: one plpgsql function `fin_assert_period_open()` returning trigger with `RAISE EXCEPTION 'ATLAS_PERIOD_CLOSED'`, attached by two CREATE TRIGGER statements. SQLite: two CREATE TRIGGER ... BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT,'ATLAS_PERIOD_CLOSED') WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fin_fiscal_periods p WHERE p.tenant_id=NEW.tenant_id AND p.status='OPEN' AND NEW.posting_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date); END. Also: the entry's stored `fiscal_period_id` is resolved by the service from posting_date and the trigger re-derives by date, so the two cannot disagree. Service layer (finance/service/periods.py) performs the same check first and raises a domain `PeriodClosedError`→HTTP 422; the trigger is the bypass-proof backstop, surfaced by mapping IntegrityError/DBAPIError messages containing the 'ATLAS_' token in core/exceptions.py. Period close/reopen are service actions gated by permissions `finance.period.close` / `finance.period.reopen`, audited; closing refuses while DRAFT entries dated in the period exist (service-level check only). Reversal entries obey the same trigger — reversing into a closed period is impossible by construction.
decisions.rationale: CLAUDE.md rule 8 demands rejection 'at service AND DB level'. Triggers are the only mechanism available on BOTH backends that can consult another table at write time; firing them on the status transition (not on line inserts) means draft editing stays cheap and the check runs exactly once per posting. The ATLAS_-prefixed message token gives the exception-mapping layer a stable, dialect-independent contract.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Postgres-only enforcement (RLS-style or constraint triggers) with service-only enforcement on SQLite — rejected: the test suite runs on SQLite, so DB-level guarantees would be untested where tests live. FK from entries to a (tenant_id, period, 'OPEN') key that close-time would break — rejected: closing a period would have to mutate/delete the referenced row and would retroactively invalidate existing posted entries' FKs. Application-level-only enforcement — rejected by hard constraint. Storing only fiscal_period_id and trigger-checking that row's status without date re-derivation — rejected as weaker: a service bug could attach a wrong open period to an out-of-range date; date-based lookup closes that hole.
decisions.risks: Trigger-vs-service divergence over time (e.g., a future period-13 adjustment rule added only in Python) — mitigated by the rule that every change to period semantics ships service code + new trigger revision + the raw-SQL bypass test in the same PR. SQLite RAISE(ABORT) surfaces as a generic OperationalError; the exceptions mapper matches on the ATLAS_PERIOD_CLOSED substring, which the tests pin.

decisions.title: Money representation (exact storage on both backends, rounding, quantities)
decisions.decision: All monetary and quantity columns use two TypeDecorators defined once in core/models.py: `MoneyType` and `QuantityType`. On PostgreSQL they compile to NUMERIC(18,6); on SQLite they compile to INTEGER storing scaled micro-units (Decimal × 10^6, exact integer arithmetic), with process_bind_param/process_result_value converting to/from `decimal.Decimal`. This supersedes the 'Numeric for money' example wording in D-003, because SQLAlchemy's plain Numeric on SQLite round-trips through float and silently loses precision — unacceptable when DB triggers compare exact sums. FX rates use NUMERIC(20,10) (RateType decorator, same micro-scaling at 10^10 on SQLite). Aggregations always go through SQLAlchemy Core expressions (`func.sum(JournalLine.functional_debit_amount)`) so the column's type inference applies result conversion on both backends; raw textual SQL against money columns is banned (enforced by review + a grep check in the structure self-check). Python-side: only `decimal.Decimal` ever represents money; float is banned for money/quantity in backend code (ruff custom rule via flake8-banned-api style check on `float(` around money names is best-effort; the binding gate is Pydantic). Pydantic v2 schemas declare `Decimal` fields with `Field(max_digits=18, decimal_places=...)`; JSON serializes Decimal as string (Pydantic v2 default in JSON mode), and frontend treats money as strings formatted exclusively in lib/format.ts. Rounding rules: amounts are quantized at the posting/pricing boundary to the currency's `decimal_places` from `fin_currencies` (ISO 4217: JPY=0, USD=2, BHD=3) using `Decimal.quantize(exp, rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)` (commercial rounding); stored journal amounts therefore never carry sub-minor-unit digits even though columns have scale-6 headroom. Unit prices, unit costs, and FX rates keep full scale (no premature rounding). Allocations/distributions (tax split, payment allocation, cost allocation cycles) use the largest-remainder method: round each part half-up, then assign the residual minor units to the largest line so parts always sum exactly to the total. Quantities: QuantityType scale 6 (covers UoM conversions and FIFO consumption math exactly); display precision per item UoM is frontend formatting only. Why floats are banned (recorded rationale): binary floats cannot represent most decimal fractions, so debit==credit and layer-consumption invariants would fail nondeterministically, DB trigger sum checks would require epsilon comparisons (meaningless in accounting), and audit/reversal equality would break.
decisions.rationale: The financial engine's DB-level invariants (balance trigger, exactly-one-of CHECK, valuation math) only mean something if storage is exact on BOTH backends. Integer micro-units are the standard exact representation where a true decimal type is absent, and 10^6 scaling gives one uniform contract for money and quantities. ROUND_HALF_UP matches commercial/SAP practice and user expectations on invoices.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Plain sa.Numeric everywhere — rejected: float round-trip on SQLite makes exact trigger sums and tests flaky; SQLAlchemy itself warns about Decimal on SQLite. TEXT storage of decimals on SQLite — rejected: SUM() over TEXT does float math in SQLite, breaking projections and triggers. Banker's rounding (ROUND_HALF_EVEN) — rejected: statistically nicer but surprises users reconciling invoices/tax and diverges from SAP's commercial rounding; consistency with user-facing documents wins. Storing minor units on Postgres too — rejected: NUMERIC is native, exact, human-readable in psql, and keeps PG-side raw SQL/BI friendly.
decisions.risks: Dialect-asymmetric storage means hand-written SQLite trigger SQL operates on integers while PG SQL operates on NUMERIC — comparisons (sums, >0) are semantically identical, but any future trigger doing division or scaling must be written per-dialect with care; mitigated by the per-dialect trigger convention already in place and bypass tests on both backends. 18,6 caps amounts at ~999 trillion micro-units on SQLite (int64 max ~9.2e18 = 9.2e12 units) — ample for demo/tests; PG runtime has full NUMERIC range.

decisions.title: FX handling (rates table, posting-time translation, realized vs unrealized, revaluation run)
decisions.decision: Rates table `fin_exchange_rates`: `id`, `tenant_id`, `rate_date`, `from_currency_code`, `to_currency_code`, `rate_type` string enum SPOT|CLOSING (SPOT defaults postings, CLOSING drives revaluation), `rate` NUMERIC(20,10), UNIQUE (tenant_id, rate_date, from_currency_code, to_currency_code, rate_type). Lookup semantics in finance/service/fx.py `get_rate(tenant, from_ccy, to_ccy, on_date, rate_type)`: most recent rate with rate_date <= on_date; missing rate raises MissingExchangeRateError (postings never guess and never invert pairs implicitly — store both directions or compute inverse explicitly in the service with documented 10-dp rounding). Translation happens exactly once, at posting time: the posting service resolves the SPOT rate for posting_date (or accepts a caller-supplied documented rate, stored on the header as `exchange_rate`), computes functional_debit/credit per line (quantize half-up to functional currency decimals), forces functional balance via the rounding-difference line, and freezes everything — posted lines are never re-translated (immutability triggers guarantee it). Realized FX: arises only at clearing. The open-item clearing service (AP payment applied to vendor bill, AR receipt applied to customer invoice, in finance/service/payments.py) computes, per cleared document, functional-at-invoice-rate minus functional-at-payment-rate for the cleared transaction-currency amount and posts the difference inside the same clearing journal entry to configured `fx_realized_gain` / `fx_realized_loss` accounts (account mapping rows in a `fin_posting_defaults` table keyed by purpose string, per tenant). Unrealized FX: a period-end revaluation run `run_fx_revaluation(period_id, rate_date)` in finance/service/fx.py — for each foreign-currency open item (unc leared AP/AR) and each foreign-currency bank/cash account, compute open transaction-currency balance × CLOSING rate minus carried functional value; post ONE journal entry per (currency, account) delta: balance-sheet adjustment account against `fx_unrealized_gain`/`fx_unrealized_loss` (document_type=FX_REVAL), and immediately create its reversal dated day 1 of the next period (auto-reversing pattern, so subsequent realized calculations at clearing remain based on original invoice rates and nothing double-counts). Run bookkeeping: `fin_revaluation_runs` (tenant_id, period_id, rate_date, status, created entries linked via docflow); re-running a period requires the service to first post reversals of the previous run's entries (append-only — never delete), then repost.
decisions.rationale: Matches the parity contract exactly: 'transaction + functional currency with rates table and realized/unrealized FX accounts.' Posting-time translation with frozen functional amounts is what makes the universal journal projectable without rate joins, and the auto-reversing unrealized pattern is the textbook (and SAP) approach that keeps unrealized adjustments from contaminating realized results. Purpose-keyed posting defaults keep account wiring data-driven (RBAC-as-data spirit) rather than hardcoded.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Storing only transaction amounts and translating in reports — rejected: every projection would need rate joins, historical statements would mutate when rates are edited, and the parity doc's later path (extra frozen currency columns) presumes posting-time translation. Persistent (non-reversing) unrealized revaluation that rebases item carrying value — rejected for v1: requires per-item revaluation history to keep realized math correct at clearing; auto-reversal achieves correct statements with far less machinery. Triangulation through a base currency — rejected: v1 has one functional currency per tenant, direct pairs suffice.
decisions.risks: Clearing math must use the same open-item granularity as revaluation or gains double-count — mitigated by the auto-reversal (revaluation never touches item carrying values) and a test proving invoice→revalue→reverse→pay yields total FX = invoice-rate-vs-payment-rate difference exactly. Missing-rate failures at posting time can block operational flows; acceptable and intended (fail loud), with rates seeded in seed.py.

decisions.title: Inventory costing (moving average + FIFO layers, COGS-in-same-transaction, no negative stock)
decisions.decision: Costing method per item: `inv_items.costing_method` enum MOVING_AVERAGE|FIFO (defaulted from item category, changeable only while no stock exists). Quantity SSOT remains `inv_stock_moves`. Moving average: `inv_item_valuations` (tenant_id, item_id, warehouse_id, on_hand_qty QuantityType, avg_unit_cost MoneyType scale-6 unrounded headroom, total_value MoneyType; UNIQUE (tenant_id, item_id, warehouse_id)). Every valuated move updates this row in the SAME transaction using `select(...).with_for_update()` on Postgres (row lock serializes concurrent movers; SQLite is single-writer so the same code degrades safely). Receipt: total_value += receipt_value; on_hand_qty += qty; avg_unit_cost = total_value/on_hand_qty (full precision, not rounded). Issue: cogs = quantize(qty × avg_unit_cost, currency dp, HALF_UP); total_value -= cogs; when on_hand_qty reaches 0, any residual total_value is flushed to the price-difference account so value and quantity never disagree. FIFO: `inv_cost_layers` (id, tenant_id, item_id, warehouse_id, receipt_move_id FK, received_at, original_qty, remaining_qty QuantityType CHECK remaining_qty >= 0 AND remaining_qty <= original_qty, unit_cost MoneyType) plus `inv_layer_consumptions` (issue_move_id, layer_id, qty, cost) for traceability. Partial issues consume layers ordered by (received_at, id) ascending under with_for_update(): decrement remaining_qty layer by layer until the issue quantity is covered, writing one consumption row per touched layer; COGS = sum of per-layer qty × unit_cost, each quantized, summed exactly. Reversing/cancelling an issue replays consumption rows backwards (restores remaining_qty on the exact layers); returns-to-vendor consume layers normally, customer returns create a new layer at the original COGS cost. COGS posting consistency: the in-process event bus dispatches synchronously within the SAME SQLAlchemy AsyncSession/transaction — inventory service writes the stock move + valuation/layer updates, publishes `inventory.stock.issued` carrying the computed cost; finance/handlers.py handles it by posting the COGS journal entry (Dr COGS / Cr Inventory, dimensions copied from the move: item, warehouse, cost center/WBS if assigned) before commit. One commit = move + valuation + journal + docflow link, atomic; a stock move can never exist without its journal entry or vice versa. This same-transaction coupling is an explicit v1 decision recorded for the future Kafka swap (which will introduce a transactional outbox at that point, not now). Negative stock policy: forbidden outright in v1 — service raises InsufficientStockError pre-flight, and DB CHECKs back it (`on_hand_qty >= 0` on inv_item_valuations, `remaining_qty >= 0` on layers); no per-warehouse opt-in flag. Shortage handling belongs to ATP/backorders at the sales layer per the parity doc.
decisions.rationale: Parity doc commits to 'moving average AND FIFO per item category with event-driven COGS posting.' Same-transaction event handling is the only design that keeps the financial invariant (stock value in journal == valuation table) without building outbox/reconciliation machinery the v1 scope doesn't include — and the event-bus abstraction still decouples the modules at the code level as CLAUDE.md rule 6 requires. Layer consumption rows make COGS auditable per layer and make reversals exact instead of recomputed. Banning negative stock makes FIFO well-defined (you cannot consume a layer that doesn't exist) and keeps valuation CHECKs simple.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Async/after-commit COGS posting — rejected for v1: opens a window where stock and GL disagree, requiring reconciliation jobs that contradict the no-reconciliation philosophy of the universal journal. Negative-stock allowance with provisional cost and retroactive correction (Odoo-style) — rejected: requires retroactive revaluation entries and clashes with posted-entry immutability. Single global valuation row per item (no warehouse dimension) — rejected: parity scope is multi-warehouse, and per-warehouse valuation is needed for transfer postings. Recomputing FIFO COGS from layers at report time — rejected: COGS must be a posted journal fact, not a projection, or statements would change as layers mutate.
decisions.risks: Synchronous in-transaction handlers mean a finance bug rolls back inventory operations — intended (correctness over availability) but must be documented for operators; mitigated by tight tests on the handler path. with_for_update() ordering across valuation rows could deadlock under concurrency — mitigated by always locking in (item_id, warehouse_id) sort order within a transaction. Moving-average drift from rounding is absorbed by the zero-quantity flush rule and a price-difference account, tested explicitly.

decisions.title: Custom fields: JSONB + metadata registry portable to SQLite
decisions.decision: Every extensible entity (item, vendor, customer, journal entry header, sales/purchase documents, employee, equipment — list maintained in the industry module) gets one column `custom_fields` declared once via a core/models.py helper: `sa.JSON(none_as_null=False).with_variant(postgresql.JSONB(), 'postgresql')`, NOT NULL, server_default '{}', wrapped in `MutableDict.as_mutable(...)` so in-place updates are change-tracked. Metadata registry owned by the industry module: `ind_custom_field_defs` (id, tenant_id, entity_key string like 'inventory.item', field_key snake_case validated by regex ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,49}$, label, field_type enum TEXT|NUMBER|DECIMAL|BOOLEAN|DATE|SELECT, is_required, options JSON for SELECT, validation JSON {min,max,regex,max_length}, display_group, display_order, is_active; UNIQUE (tenant_id, entity_key, field_key)). Defs are written by industry-template application at tenant provisioning and by an admin CRUD endpoint (/api/v1/industry/custom-field-defs). Validation path: owning-module services call `validate_custom_fields(session, tenant_id, entity_key, payload) -> dict` exposed in modules/industry/queries.py (the one cross-module-importable file per STRUCTURE §5 — it is a read+pure-validate helper, no writes, so it belongs there; recorded as the sanctioned interpretation). It loads active defs (cached per-request), rejects unknown keys, enforces required-on-create, coerces and validates per type: DATE = ISO-8601 string, DECIMAL = string parsed via Decimal (never JSON float — consistent with the money decision), NUMBER = int, BOOLEAN = bool, SELECT membership in options. Pydantic schemas type the field as `custom_fields: dict[str, Any] = {}` and the service validator is the gate (schema-level dynamic models rejected — defs are per-tenant data, not import-time code). Report-builder surfacing: the reporting module reads defs via industry/queries.py to offer custom fields as columns/filters; query construction uses SQLAlchemy's portable JSON path operators — `Model.custom_fields['field_key'].as_string()` / `.as_integer()` / `.as_boolean()` — which render `->>` on PostgreSQL and `JSON_EXTRACT()` on SQLite, with `sa.cast` per field_type (DECIMAL fields cast via the string value through Numeric for ordering/aggregation on PG; on SQLite report sorting on DECIMAL custom fields uses CAST to REAL and is documented as display-grade, not financial-grade). Indexing: optional per-entity GIN index on the JSONB column created in a Postgres-only Alembic branch when an industry template declares searchable fields; SQLite gets none (demo scale).
decisions.rationale: Fulfills the parity doc's 'Metadata-driven field extensibility surfaced across the UI — Full' commitment with exactly the JSONB+registry design it names. One nullable-free JSON column per entity keeps Alembic migrations trivial when templates add fields (no DDL per field). Routing validation through the owning service keeps the service-layer-owns-logic rule intact while the registry stays industry-module property. The SQLAlchemy variant + portable JSON path API is the only part of the stack where PG/SQLite JSON differences surface, and it confines them to two call sites.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: EAV table (entity_id, field_id, value) — rejected: row-explosion, painful report queries, no document-shaped reads. Dynamic ALTER TABLE per custom field (real columns) — rejected: per-tenant DDL is operationally dangerous and impossible to express in linear Alembic history. Dynamically generated Pydantic models per tenant — rejected: defs are runtime data; building models at request time adds caching complexity for zero gain over a dict validator. Storing DECIMAL custom values as JSON numbers — rejected: floats by another name.
decisions.risks: Custom fields are invisible to DB constraints — accepted: they are descriptive/reporting fields by design; anything participating in financial invariants must be a real column (rule recorded in docs/modules/industry.md). JSON_EXTRACT semantics differ subtly from ->> for nested values — mitigated by restricting keys to flat top-level scalars (registry enforces no nesting). Field deletion orphans stored values — defs get is_active soft-deactivation, never hard delete.

decisions.title: Alembic dual-database strategy and CI matrix
decisions.decision: Single linear migration chain runs unmodified on both backends; migrations are the ONLY schema source — `Base.metadata.create_all` is banned everywhere including tests, because triggers and raw DDL live only in migrations (tests would otherwise pass without the DB guards they claim to test). backend/tests/conftest.py runs `alembic upgrade head` (via `asyncio` + `run_sync` on the aiosqlite engine, programmatic `alembic.command.upgrade` with Config pointed at a per-session temp file DB) once per test session. Concrete rules: (1) env.py uses the async pattern (`async_engine_from_config` + `connection.run_sync(do_run_migrations)`), reads ATLAS_DATABASE_URL, and sets `context.configure(compare_type=True, render_as_batch=True)` so autogenerate emits batch-compatible ops. (2) Every ALTER goes through `with op.batch_alter_table('table') as batch_op:` unconditionally — pass-through DDL on Postgres, copy-rebuild on SQLite. This requires deterministic constraint names: core/models.py declares `MetaData(naming_convention={'ix':'ix_%(column_0_label)s','uq':'uq_%(table_name)s_%(column_0_name)s','ck':'ck_%(table_name)s_%(constraint_name)s','fk':'fk_%(table_name)s_%(column_0_name)s_%(referred_table_name)s','pk':'pk_%(table_name)s'})` — without named constraints SQLite batch mode cannot drop/recreate them. (3) Type portability lives in the models (JSONB via `.with_variant`, sa.Uuid, MoneyType/QuantityType TypeDecorators), so autogenerated migrations import those types from app.core.models and stay dialect-clean; hand review of every autogen revision is mandatory (STRUCTURE §8.6). (4) Trigger and function DDL: per-dialect string pairs in the migration body, executed under `bind = op.get_bind(); if bind.dialect.name == 'postgresql': op.execute(PG_SQL) else: op.execute(SQLITE_SQL)`; every trigger has a stable name (trg_<table>_<purpose>), upgrades use DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS then CREATE, downgrades drop them; Postgres-only physical extras (GIN indexes, INCLUDE columns, partial-index variants where syntax differs) sit in the same dialect branch with a no-op (or plain-index) SQLite arm. (5) CI (single `backend` job per D-005, extended): step A runs `alembic upgrade head` + full `uv run pytest -q` on SQLite (file DB); step B uses a `services: postgres:16` container and runs `alembic upgrade head`, then `alembic downgrade base && alembic upgrade head` (reversibility proof), then a marked subset `uv run pytest -q -m pg` re-exercising the DB-guard tests (triggers, JSONB paths, FOR UPDATE) against real Postgres. The `pg` marker is applied to tests/modules/finance/test_journal_db_guards.py, test_periods.py DB-bypass tests, and inventory locking tests.
decisions.rationale: D-003 fixed the dual-backend posture; this makes it mechanical. Batch-alter-everywhere plus a naming convention is the canonical Alembic recipe for SQLite compatibility, and putting type variance in model-level types (not migrations) means autogenerate output is portable by construction. Running the financial-guard tests on real Postgres in CI is what makes 'enforced at DB level on BOTH' a tested claim rather than an assertion.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Two migration branches (one per dialect) — rejected: guaranteed drift, doubles review load, breaks linear NNNN numbering in STRUCTURE §7. create_all for tests with a trigger-installation fixture — rejected: duplicates trigger DDL outside migrations, violating single-source and the no-orphan-logic spirit. Skipping Postgres in CI (docker-compose-only) — rejected: triggers and FOR UPDATE behavior differ enough that untested-on-PG is unacceptable for the financial engine. Separate .sql files for trigger DDL — rejected: STRUCTURE forbids orphan files; migration files are self-contained.
decisions.risks: Session-scoped migrated SQLite DB needs per-test isolation — solved with nested transactions/SAVEPOINT rollback per test (standard SQLAlchemy join-external-transaction pattern in conftest). Batch mode table-rebuild can silently drop SQLite triggers attached to the rebuilt table — mitigated: any migration batch-altering a trigger-bearing table must re-execute the trigger DDL afterwards; this rule is recorded in the migration template comment and covered by the pg/sqlite guard tests which run on the final migrated schema.

decisions.title: Statements as pure projections + account-type model
decisions.decision: Account model: `fin_accounts` (tenant_id, code, name, account_type string enum ASSET|LIABILITY|EQUITY|REVENUE|EXPENSE, normal_balance derived from type — debit for ASSET/EXPENSE, is_postable boolean, cash_flow_category nullable enum OPERATING|INVESTING|FINANCING, is_cash_equivalent boolean for cash-flow anchoring, account_group_id FK). `fin_account_groups` (tenant_id, code, name, parent_id self-FK, sort_order) is a pure presentation hierarchy for statement layout; only leaf accounts are postable. This typing makes every statement derivable: P&L = REVENUE+EXPENSE over a date range; BS = ASSET/LIABILITY/EQUITY cumulative to a date; since v1 has no year-end carryforward (per parity doc), the BS computes retained earnings on the fly as the cumulative REVENUE+EXPENSE net over ALL history up to the as-of date, presented as a synthetic 'Current and accumulated earnings' equity line — exact by construction. Projection mechanics: all statements are built in finance/service/statements.py (reporting consumes via finance/queries.py per the dependency rule) from ONE base aggregate over fin_journal_lines only — no header join, because lines denormalize tenant_id, posting_date, fiscal_period_id, is_posted (set during the posting transaction): `select(JournalLine.account_id, func.sum(JournalLine.functional_debit_amount - JournalLine.functional_credit_amount)).where(tenant filter, JournalLine.is_posted == True, date predicates).group_by(JournalLine.account_id)` — the MoneyType type inference keeps the sums exact on both backends. Trial balance = that query with per-account debit/credit totals split; P&L/BS = same rows joined to fin_accounts and folded through account_groups in Python; cash flow (indirect) = net income for the range + signed deltas of non-cash BS account balances between the two as-of dates grouped by cash_flow_category, reconciled to the movement on is_cash_equivalent accounts (service asserts the reconciliation to zero — a built-in self-check that the projection is consistent). No stored totals anywhere: no balance tables, no materialized views, nothing to reconcile (CLAUDE.md rule 1). Performance: composite partial index `ix_fin_journal_lines_proj ON fin_journal_lines (tenant_id, account_id, posting_date) WHERE is_posted` (partial indexes work on BOTH PG and SQLite ≥3.8); on PostgreSQL additionally `postgresql_include=['functional_debit_amount','functional_credit_amount']` makes statement queries index-only scans (SQLite arm omits INCLUDE via dialect kwarg, harmless). This holds sub-second to ~10M lines on Postgres. The recorded escape hatch if scale ever exceeds that: an explicitly-cache-semantics summary (materialized view refreshed from the journal, journal remains SSOT) — out of v1 and gated on a DECISIONS.md entry.
decisions.rationale: Direct implementation of the Universal Journal architecture rule: views are projections, totals are never stored, FI/CO reconciliation eliminated by construction. The five-type account model plus cash_flow_category is the minimal metadata from which all four statements derive mechanically; computing retained earnings from full history is what makes 'no carryforward in v1' sound rather than a correctness hole. The single base query keeps every statement provably consistent with the trial balance (same predicate, same index).
decisions.alternatives_rejected: Running-balance or period-totals tables updated on posting — rejected: violates CLAUDE.md rule 1 verbatim and reintroduces the reconciliation problem the architecture exists to kill. Statement layout encoded as account-code ranges (classic SAP FSV-by-interval) — rejected for v1: account_group FK hierarchy is simpler, referentially enforced, and template-friendly. Direct cash-flow method — rejected: requires counterparty-cash tagging on every line; indirect method derives from data already present. Materialized views in v1 — rejected: premature, PG-only, and blurs the no-stored-totals rule before scale demands it.
decisions.risks: Cumulative-from-genesis BS queries grow linearly with history until balance carryforward ships (already a parity-doc 'later') — the partial covering index keeps this an index-only scan, and the carryforward job slots in later without schema change. The is_posted denormalized flag must never disagree with header status — guaranteed by the posting-transaction ordering plus the immutability triggers (lines untouchable once the header is POSTED), and asserted by a dedicated guard test.

decisions.title: Tenancy enforcement (non-bypassable session filter)
decisions.decision: Three cooperating layers in core/tenancy.py + core/db.py. (1) Context: ContextVar[uuid.UUID | None] `current_tenant_id`, set only by `get_current_user` in core/deps.py after JWT validation (and by the refresh endpoint directly from the validated refresh-token tenant_id claim — refresh does NOT use system_context), reset via token in a finally block by a pure-ASGI middleware. (2) Read/write filtering: a global `@event.listens_for(Session, "do_orm_execute")` hook on the sync Session class (AsyncSession proxies it, so it covers all execute calls and relationship/lazy loads) adds `with_loader_criteria(TenantMixin, lambda cls: cls.tenant_id == current_tenant_id.get(), include_aliases=True, track_closure_variables=False)` to every ORM statement, including ORM-enabled update()/delete(). FAIL-CLOSED: if the statement touches any TenantMixin mapper and `current_tenant_id` is unset, raise TenancyError — unless the `system_context()` ContextVar (also in core/tenancy.py) is active; system_context is invoked in exactly four greppable places: login user-lookup, tenant provisioning in admin, Alembic/seed provisioning phase, and bus system-event replay. (3) Write stamping: a `before_flush` listener stamps tenant_id on new TenantMixin objects when unset and raises TenancyError when a new/dirty object's tenant_id differs from the context. (4) DB backstop: every FK between tenant-scoped tables is composite `(tenant_id, <entity>_id)` referencing `UNIQUE (tenant_id, id)` on the parent, declared via a `tenant_fk()` helper in core/models.py. CRITICAL SQLite fix: SQLite only enforces FKs with `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`, so core/db.py registers an engine `connect` event that emits the pragma on every SQLite connection (runtime, tests, seed) — without this the backstop silently does nothing on the test engine. Core-level statements (Core Table inserts, text()) bypass the ORM hook; they are sanctioned only inside core/ (audit writer, numbering, idempotency) where tenant_id is always explicit, enforced by a CI grep gate banning `text(` and Core `.insert(` under app/modules/ (tests/ is exempt — DB-guard tests need raw SQL). Non-bypassability tests in tests/core/test_tenancy.py iterate `Base.registry.mappers` so new models are auto-covered: for every TenantMixin mapper assert (a) bare select() under tenant A returns zero tenant-B rows, (b) relationship loads never leak, (c) ORM update() with no WHERE touches only tenant-A rows, (d) execution with unset ContextVar raises, (e) inserting a foreign tenant_id raises, (f) session.get(cls, b_id) under tenant A returns None.
decisions.rationale: do_orm_execute + with_loader_criteria is the only SQLAlchemy 2.0 mechanism that injects criteria into every ORM statement — including lazy loads and bulk ORM writes — with zero cooperation from query authors, which is the literal 'cannot bypass' requirement. ContextVar is async-task-safe under FastAPI. Fail-closed converts 'forgot to set tenant' from a leak into a hard error. Composite FKs give a schema-level invariant on both engines, but only if the SQLite FK pragma is actually on — the original draft omitted that, which would have made the backstop a no-op exactly where CI runs. Mapper-enumerating tests make the guarantee self-extending.
decisions.alternatives_rejected: PostgreSQL RLS with SET LOCAL app.tenant_id: unprovable in the SQLite CI/demo run, so it cannot be the primary mechanism; noted in DECISIONS.md as Postgres-only hardening post-v1. Per-query .where() helpers or custom Query base: bypassable by anyone writing select() directly. Schema- or database-per-tenant: contradicts the mandated row-level design and makes provisioning/Alembic disproportionately heavy. Mapper write-events only: guards writes, not reads.
decisions.risks: Raw SQL and Core statements bypass the hook — bounded by the grep gate, the composite-FK backstop, and review; residual gap recorded in DECISIONS.md. Identity-map hits (session.get) skip SQL — benign because the request-scoped session only ever holds same-tenant rows; sessions are never shared across requests. track_closure_variables=False is mandatory so the lambda re-reads the ContextVar per execution instead of baking in the first value seen; a dedicated test executes the same statement under two tenants in one process to pin this.

decisions.title: Auth token flow (JWT access+refresh, rotation with grace window, argon2)
decisions.decision: PyJWT, HS256, single `ATLAS_SECRET_KEY` (env, >=64 random bytes). Access token: 15-min TTL, claims {sub: user_id, tenant_id, sid: refresh-session id, ver: user.token_version, typ: 'access', jti, iat, exp}; stateless, but `ver` is compared against core_users.token_version (the user row is loaded anyway for RBAC), so 'revoke everything' = increment token_version. No permissions in the token. Refresh token: JWT, 14-day TTL, claims {sub, tenant_id, sid, typ: 'refresh', jti, exp}, delivered as an httpOnly Secure SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to path /api/v1/auth; the access token is returned in the JSON body and held in SPA memory only. Server state: core_refresh_sessions (id uuid = sid, tenant_id, user_id, current_jti_hash sha256, prev_jti_hash sha256 nullable, rotated_at, issued_at, last_used_at, expires_at, revoked_at nullable, ip, user_agent).
